figures.caption: Figure 1: AMRS architecture. Top: the offline training pipeline (dashed boundary); the trained policy is then deployed to production. Bottom: a logged session has engagement and (optional) ratings per song with valence-arousal observations only at session boundaries (post-session optional); a world-model rollout produces all four predictions (𝑒, 𝑟, 𝑣, 𝑎) at every step. This sparse-vs-dense affective contrast motivates the rollout-based world model.

Table 2: World-model results across architecture and embedding configurations. Mean (SD) over 10 MCCV test splits. PE = rotary positional encoding [22]. Bold = best per-metric mean; shaded row = overall-best configuration by equal-weight average rank. Stars: paired 𝑡-test vs. shaded row (∗𝑝 < 0.05, ∗∗𝑝 < 0.01, ∗∗∗𝑝 < 0.001).

Table 3: Leave-one-feature-out ablation on the factorized MERT (no-PE) world-model base. Each row removes one input during both training and test. Mean (SD) over 10 MCCV test splits. Bold = best per-metric mean. Stars: paired 𝑡-test vs. base (∗𝑝 < 0.05, ∗∗𝑝 < 0.01, ∗∗∗𝑝 < 0.001).

Table 4: Predicted feedback and diversity across recommendation policies (window strategy, test split, 𝐿=5 songs, 𝑁=5 seeds). Rating and engagement are held out of the DPO objective and shown as a no-degradation check. Cross-seed mean (SD). Bold = best among learned policies (Copycat, DPO). Stars: paired 𝑡-test vs. DPO (∗𝑝 < 0.05, ∗∗𝑝 < 0.01, ∗∗∗𝑝 < 0.001).

Table 5: Policy adherence under the window strategy (𝑁=5 seeds). Level 2 (user-wise): an item is relevant if it appears in the user’s logged history. Level 3 (time-step): an item is relevant only if it matches the exact song at the same time step. Values are cross-seed means. Cross-seed SDs are ≤ 0.005 at Level 3; at Level 2, ≤ 0.05 on train/test and ≤ 0.08 on validation. Highest value per row in bold.
